name: Baumol's Cost Disease
statement: Wages rise in jobs that never get more efficient, so their cost keeps climbing.
meaning: In labour-intensive sectors with little productivity growth — live performance, teaching, nursing — wages rise anyway, because those sectors must compete for workers with high-productivity sectors where wages are rising. The result is that the cost, and relative price, of such services climbs steadily over time without any matching gain in their output per worker.
mechanism: Some jobs grow far more productive over time; others cannot. Playing a Beethoven string quartet takes four musicians and about the same time as it did two centuries ago — productivity in live performance is essentially fixed. Yet musicians must be paid roughly competitively with workers in sectors where productivity did grow, or they leave. So wages across the economy rise together, driven by productivity gains concentrated in manufacturing and technology, while the stagnant services see rising wages with no productivity offset — and their prices must rise or the gap be subsidised.

examples.text: The original case Baumol and Bowen documented — orchestras, opera, theatre, and dance face rising per-performance costs and chronic funding gaps, since a live performance cannot be made more efficient without destroying the product.

The most-studied modern application: care is labour-intensive and hard to speed up, and a substantial literature finds Baumol effects significant in health-spending growth, though the magnitude is debated.
Teaching is labour-intensive with limited productivity gains, so rising college and school costs are often attributed to the cost disease — though how much it explains is contested.

variants.name: Effect versus disease
variants.text: Some economists prefer 'Baumol effect' to 'cost disease,' arguing the rising relative price of stagnant-sector services is a natural, even benign, consequence of growth rather than a pathology.

variants.name: Unbalanced growth
variants.text: The macro framework Baumol formalised in 1967 — an economy split into progressive and stagnant sectors growing at systematically different productivity rates, driving a rising service share of output.

whyItMatters: It explains one of the most persistent features of rich economies: why the prices of services like health, education, and the arts rise faster than goods, decade after decade. It reframes that rise not as waste but as an unavoidable by-product of productivity growth elsewhere, and shows a richer society can still afford these services precisely because other sectors grew more efficient.

working.text: in labour-intensive services that resist automation, anticipate rising relative costs even with no fall in quality or efficiency.

working.lead: Blame the wage link, not waste
working.text: read climbing service costs as the pull of competitive wages from productive sectors, not necessarily as mismanagement.
for any specific sector, treat the cost disease as one contributor alongside subsidies, administration, and technology, not the whole story.

limits: The core mechanism — an inverse relation between a sector's productivity growth and its relative price growth — is documented, formalised in a testable two-sector model, and commands fairly strong expert agreement. But how much of any particular sector's cost growth it explains is genuinely contested. In higher education, critics argue its role is overstated relative to declining public subsidies and administrative growth. In health care, major technological change complicates the assumption of stagnant productivity, and some argue the disease affects long-term care more than high-tech acute care. Service-sector productivity is also hard to measure, which may bias judgements of how stagnant these sectors truly are.
misreadings: It does not say the affected sectors are badly run or that their rising cost is avoidable waste — the rise follows from competitive wages, not inefficiency. And it does not by itself 'explain' rising college or hospital costs in full; its share of the explanation is an open empirical question.
origin: Identified by the economists William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen in their 1966 study Performing Arts, The Economic Dilemma, and formalised in Baumol's 'Macroeconomics of Unbalanced Growth,' American Economic Review 57(3):415-426 (1967); Baumol extended it to health and education in a 2012 book.

sources.text: Baumol effect, Wikipedia. — the productivity-lag mechanism, the string-quartet illustration, and the 1966/1967 origin.
"Diagnosing William Baumol's Cost Disease," Chicago Booth Review. — the quartet framing, expert agreement, and the health/education debates.
